claims.text: For near-equiatomic nanoparticles containing at least five metals, structural and chemical stability from 473 to 1923 K is primarily governed by the degree of atomic mixing.
High atomic mixing resists phase segregation.
During in situ vacuum annealing, initially well-mixed nanoparticles will undergo less diffusion-driven phase separation than nanoparticles with slight initial compositional inhomogeneity.
The relevant initial material is a uniform solid-solution nanoparticle containing near-equal proportions of at least five metals.
Gradual heating under high vacuum across 473–1923 K ensures thermal equilibrium.
Uniform atomic dispersion and the absence of local lattice distortions mediate nanoparticle stability.
Elevated temperature facilitates surface diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Elevated temperature facilitates lattice diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Thermally activated surface and lattice diffusion can drive phase segregation and local ordering changes.
High atomic mixing suppresses diffusion-mediated segregation and ordering changes, preserving the solid-solution state.
Preservation of the well-mixed solid-solution state maintains uniform catalytic and thermoelectric properties.
Initially uniform nanoparticles will retain structural and chemical homogeneity with minimal phase-boundary formation or segregation up to temperatures approaching 1923 K.
Initially inhomogeneous controls will exhibit observable phase segregation and surface-diffusion-related alterations at high temperatures.
The as-synthesized baseline has a uniform atomic distribution confirmed by high-resolution STEM and compositional mapping.
Exposure to ambient gases may cause behavior that deviates from the predicted vacuum stability.
Rapid heating may cause behavior that deviates from the prediction under controlled heating.
The temperature at which diffusion-driven segregation becomes significant depends on the identities and interactions of the constituent metals.
